Issues.Title: System.IO.FileFormatException when printing documents containing Calibri family fonts in .NET 11
Issues.Body:
### Description

We are encountering a printing issue in .NET 11 when printing documents that contain specific font families. 

During the print operation, the following exception is thrown:
_System.IO.FileFormatException: File 'file:///C:/WINDOWS/FONTS/CALIBRI.TTF' has an invalid file format._

The exception occurs during the following call:
_printDialog.PrintDocument(documentPaginator, printDescription);_

This issue is reproducible only in .NET 11 and does not occur in .NET 10 when using the same application and printing logic. We verified the behavior on multiple machines and were able
to reproduce the issue consistently.

The following font families are known to trigger the exception:

- Calibri
- Cambria
- Cambria Math
- Constantia
- Corbel



### Reproduction Steps

1.	Run the attached sample application.
2.	Click the "Print" button.
3.	The Print dialog will open. Print the document as PDF.
4.	A System.IO.FileFormatException is thrown.
5.	Please refer to the attached video for a detailed illustration of the issue.

[Print issues - NET11-Application.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34181257/Print.issues.-.NET11-Application.zip)

[NET11 Print issue - Video.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34181265/NET11.Print.issue.-.Video.zip)

### Expected behavior

Documents containing the above font families should print successfully without throwing any exceptions.

### Actual behavior

The print operation fails with a `System.IO.FileFormatException`, indicating that the font file has an invalid file format.

### Regression?

Yes. Working fine in .NET 10
Break in .NET 11

### Known Workarounds

### Impact

### Configuration

.NET 11
Windows
WPF sample

Issues.Title: Use Platforms dependency for runtime installation
Issues.Body:
Related to #12039. <!-- Issue Number -->

Main PR: this PR ports the release/11.0 fix from #12039. <!-- Link to PR if any that fixed this in the main branch. -->

## Description

<!-- Give a brief summary of the issue and how the pull request is fixing it. -->

Track Microsoft.NETCore.Platforms from the same VMR snapshot as the existing runtime dependencies and use MicrosoftNETCorePlatformsVersion for x64 and x86 runtime installation.

Unlike Microsoft.NETCore.App.Ref, Platforms retains its build-stamped version when packages stabilize. This preserves the build-specific runtime download directory used by dotnet-install. The current main runtime build remains 12.0.0-alpha.1.26519.114.

## Customer Impact

<!-- What is the impact to customers of not taking this fix? -->

Prevents build/bootstrap failures when the reference pack stabilizes before release-version runtime download directories are available. No shipped runtime behavior or public API changes.

## Regression

<!-- Is this fixing a problem that was introduced in the most recent release, ie., fixing a regression? -->

No current main-branch regression; ports the fix for the release/11.0 bootstrap failure to prevent recurrence.

## Testing

<!-- What kind of testing has been done with the fix. -->

- `git diff --check` - passed.
- Temporary JSON/XML and MSBuild validation passed: dependency provenance, generated package-version property and alias, and both global.json runtime selectors resolve consistently to `12.0.0-alpha.1.26519.114`.
- Installed both runtime architectures into isolated temporary directories using the official dotnet-install script. With `$files` pointing at the temporary validation directory, both commands passed:

  ```powershell
  powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File "$files\dotnet-install.ps1" -Runtime dotnet -Version 12.0.0-alpha.1.26519.114 -Architecture x64 -AzureFeed https://ci.dot.net/public -InstallDir "$files\runtime-main-x64" -NoPath
  powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File "$files\dotnet-install.ps1" -Runtime dotnet -Version 12.0.0-alpha.1.26519.114 -Architecture x86 -AzureFeed https://ci.dot.net/public -InstallDir "$files\runtime-main-x86" -NoPath
  ```

- `dotnet.exe --list-runtimes` on each isolated installation confirmed `Microsoft.NETCore.App 12.0.0-alpha.1.26519.114`.
- Full product build and unit tests were not run; this change is limited to build bootstrap configuration.

## Risk

<!-- Please assess the risk of taking this fix. Provide details backing up your assessment. -->

Low. Only dependency metadata and runtime installation selectors change; the selected runtime build is unchanged.

Issues.Title: [release/11.0] Fix providing EnhancedMetafile to other applications through the clipboard
Issues.Body:
Fixes #11986

Depends on corresponding WinForms side of changes: https://github.com/dotnet/winforms/pull/15328
This PR has to merge before that change flows into WPF, or WPF won't build.

## Description

On .NET 10, the shared OLE code in System.Private.Windows.Core rejects every `TYMED_ENHMF` request with `DV_E_TYMED`, so WPF can't provide `CF_ENHMETAFILE` to other applications even though the format is still advertised.

- Add `WpfOleServices.AllowedTymeds`, which also allows `TYMED_ENHMF`. It implements the new `IOleServices.AllowedTymeds` from dotnet/winforms#TBD.
- Fix the `TYMED_ENHMF` branch of `WpfOleServices.GetDataHere`, which was unreachable until now. For a `MemoryStream` it never assigned the handle to the medium, so it returned `S_OK` with a null handle. It now sets `tymed` and `hEnhMetaFile`, and returns `E_FAIL` when there is no handle, as .NET 9 did.
- Add a clipboard test that reads the EMF back with `GetClipboardData`, the way another application would. It's skipped until the winforms change flows in.

I'd like to request a backport to `release/10.0` after this merges.

## Customer Impact

EMF that WPF apps put on the clipboard can't be pasted into other applications, for example Word's Paste Special → Picture (Enhanced Metafile). It fails silently, and there's no workaround.

## Regression

Yes. It works on .NET 9 and is broken on .NET 10.

## Testing

- `build.cmd -pack` succeeds, both against the current `Microsoft.Private.Winforms` package and against a local build of dotnet/winforms#15218.
- Built against dotnet/winforms#15218, the new test passes for `copy: true` and `copy: false`.
- End-to-end on .NET 11 RC 1, a test app can now read the EMF through `GetClipboardData(CF_ENHMETAFILE)` and OLE `GetData`, for delayed and flushed data. The unpatched runtime fails all three checks.
- CTI validated the change successfully

## Risk

Low. It only affects `TYMED_ENHMF` requests for `EnhancedMetafile` data, which always fail today, and restores the .NET 9 behavior.

Issues.Title: ListView DefaultListViewStyle triggers overwrite ListView behavior
Issues.Body:
### Description

The "Style.Triggers"-way of determining whether the ListView.View inherits from a GridView in the DefaultListViewStyle makes inheriting and changing the visual of GridViews practically impossible (there's a workaround, but it's ugly).

Not inheriting from GridView is a non-starter to begin with as "OnThemeChanged" is internal, and we cannot overwrite and forward that like GridView does.

### Reproduction Steps

- https://github.com/AliveDevil/dotnet-ListViewFailure
- Verify in Live Property Explorer when in System-ThemeMode on the ListView that the Template and ItemContainerStyle are replaced by "Style Triggers".

### Expected behavior

Works the same as in any other WPF theme.

### Actual behavior

Due to the Style.Triggers-setters any style provided by `ViewBase.DefaultStyleKey` or `ViewBase.ItemContainerDefaultStyleKey` is ignored, or only partially applied.

### Regression?

The default "ThemeMode=None"-behavior works, only the Fluent-Theme regressed here.

### Known Workarounds

Setting the `Style` on the ListView explicitely, and overwriting the ItemContainerStyle in that Style works:

**MainWindow.xaml**
```diff
- <ListView>
+ <ListView Style="{StaticResource {x:Static local:CustomGridView.CustomGridViewStyleKey}}">
```

**Themes/Generic.xaml**
```diff
 <Style x:Key="{x:Static local:CustomGridView.CustomGridViewStyleKey}"
        TargetType="{x:Type ListView}">
+    <Setter Property="ItemContainerStyle"
+            Value="{DynamicResource {x:Static local:CustomGridView.CustomGridViewItemContainerStyleKey}}" />
     <Setter Property="Template">
```

However, this makes ListViews with customized GridViews awkward to use.

Issues.Title: Adding Device coordinate and size
Issues.Body:
Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/wpf/issues/4127

Main PR <!-- Link to PR if any that fixed this in the main branch. -->

## Description

Adding Device coordinate and size.

`Left`/`Top` are DIP values, so WPF has to guess which monitor the value belongs to when converting back to screen pixels. That guess is ambiguous when two monitors with different scale factors contain the same DIP coordinate (dotnet/wpf#4127: both windows below report `Left == 850`). The new properties take the device value directly, so no guess is needed.

The request is applied at creation, and on change it is coalesced per frame and applied through `SetWindowPos`/`SetWindowPlacement`. It is scoped to one native placement operation by carrying the requested axes in `HwndSource.DpiSuggestedRect`, so synchronous DPI messages keep those axes while a later user resize does not. The DIP `Left`/`Top`/`Width`/`Height` paths skip only the axis that has an active device request, and `SizeToContent` plus `MinWidth`/`MaxWidth` clamping still win. The default value is `NaN`, which means "no request".

## Customer Impact

<!-- What is the impact to customers of not taking this fix? -->

Apps can place and restore windows on a specific monitor exactly at any DPI, which is currently not possible under PerMonitorV2: a window moved between monitors with different scale factors may jump or land on the wrong monitor. Without this fix there is no supported way to set the position in device units.

## Regression

<!-- Is this fixing a problem that was introduced in the most recent release, ie., fixing a regression? -->

## Testing

<!-- What kind of testing has been done with the fix. -->

## Risk

Low. The feature is additive and inactive by default; every new code path is guarded by a `NaN` check. The parts that touch existing behavior are small and reviewable in isolation: the extra optional parameter on `HwndSource.OnDpiChanged`/`HwndTarget.OnDpiChanged`, `SetupInitialState` reading bounds through `ReadDeviceBounds()` instead of `WindowBounds` directly, and the early returns added to the `On*Changed` handlers. The highest risk area is the monitor selection in `ResolveDeviceCreation`, which only runs when a device property is set.

Non-PerMonitorV2 processes (system DPI aware or unaware) are largely unaffected:

- No `WM_DPICHANGED` is sent, so the `HwndSource.DpiSuggestedRect` plumbing is never consulted; only the explicit `SetWindowPos`/`SetWindowPlacement` calls run, and those are the same calls `Left`/`Top`/`Width`/`Height` already make.
- The values follow `GetWindowRect` semantics, so they are plain OS-reported coordinates. In an unaware or system-aware process that means they can be DPI-virtualized on monitors whose DPI differs from the awareness DPI, exactly as `GetWindowRect` is today. No extra conversion is added on the device-only path.
- One caveat: when only some axes are requested, `ResolveDeviceCreation` fills the remaining axes from the logical values using the effective DPI of the selected monitor. In a non-PMv2 process whose awareness DPI differs from that monitor's DPI, such a mixed request can size slightly differently than the pure DIP path. It is only reachable when a device property is set, and the pure DIP path (all `NaN`) is untouched.

Issues.Title: HwndHost disposed while connected to a window is never collected: HwndSource keeps its keyboard input site
Issues.Body:
## Description

If an `HwndHost` is disposed while it is still in a window's visual tree, and then removed from the tree, the window's `HwndSource` keeps the host's `HwndSourceKeyboardInputSite` in its keyboard sink list for as long as the window lives. The host and everything it references can never be collected. In an application, the window is usually the main window, so every host torn down in that order leaks.

This affects every `HwndHost` subclass: `WindowsFormsHost`, the WPF `WebBrowser`, WebView2's WPF control and custom hosts. Disposing a host before detaching it is the natural order when a view is closed. For example, a document view disposes its browser when the document closes, and the docking framework detaches the view afterwards.

## Cause

In `HwndHost.cs`, only `OnSourceChanged` unregisters the keyboard input site:

```csharp
IKeyboardInputSite keyboardInputSite = ((IKeyboardInputSink)this).KeyboardInputSite;
if (keyboardInputSite != null)
{
    ((IKeyboardInputSink)this).KeyboardInputSite = null;
    keyboardInputSite.Unregister();
}
```

`Dispose(bool disposing)` removes the `SourceChanged` handler (`PresentationSource.RemoveSourceChangedHandler(this, OnSourceChanged)`) but does not unregister the site. After disposal, removing the host from the tree no longer reaches `OnSourceChanged`, so the site is never unregistered. The `IKeyboardInputSink.KeyboardInputSite` documentation says the site "should be set to null before disposal", but `HwndHost.Dispose` does not do that itself.


### Reproduction Steps

A minimal WPF app with no package references is attached (`HwndHostKeyboardSiteRetentionRepro`). It hosts a one-window `HwndHost` (a Win32 `STATIC` child) in a window that stays open, tears it down, forces a full GC, and counts survivors through `WeakReference`:

```csharp
var host = new NativeHost();                 // HwndHost creating a STATIC child window
window.Content = new Grid { Children = { host } };
Pump();                                      // host is now registered as a keyboard input sink

host.Dispose();                              // dispose while still connected...
window.Content = null;                       // ...then detach
Pump();
// force full GC: host survives
```

Run it with `dotnet run -c Debug`, or with `--auto` to print the result without a message box.

### Expected behavior

The host is collected after it is disposed and removed from the tree, whatever the order. `HwndHost.Dispose` should unregister its keyboard input site, as `OnSourceChanged` does.

### Actual behavior

Three cycles of each order, with the window kept open:

```
Surviving hosts after each cycle (3 cycles, window kept open):
  RemoveThenDispose                      0 -> 0 -> 0   (entries left in HwndSource keyboard-site list: 0)
  DisposeThenRemove                      1 -> 2 -> 3   (entries left in HwndSource keyboard-site list: 3)
  UnregisterSiteThenDisposeThenRemove    0 -> 0 -> 0   (entries left in HwndSource keyboard-site list: 0)
```

The retention path is `HwndSource._keyboardInputSinkChildren` → `HwndSourceKeyboardInputSite` → host. In a larger application we also confirmed this path with `dotnet-dump gcroot` for WebView2's WPF control.

### Regression?

Not known. Not tested on .NET Framework.

### Known Workarounds

Unregister the site before disposing:

```csharp
((IKeyboardInputSink)host).KeyboardInputSite?.Unregister();
host.Dispose();
```

Alternatively, remove the host from the tree before disposing it.

### Impact

_No response_

### Configuration

- .NET 10.0.13 (`net10.0-windows`, `UseWPF`)
- Windows 11, build 10.0.26200, x64
- Not specific to a configuration, as far as known



### Other information

A November 2021 comment on MicrosoftEdge/WebView2Feedback#1633 suspected `HwndSourceKeyboardInputSite` was keeping WebView2's WPF control alive after `Dispose()`. That issue was closed for an unrelated WinUI fix, and we found no dotnet/wpf issue for it.

A possible fix is to unregister the site in `HwndHost.Dispose(bool disposing)` (when `disposing` is true), using the same code as `OnSourceChanged`.
